title: how auto sector could be driving force bid scale plastic recycling  ecmii 2026 09 03
text:
September 3 - Every year, more than 800,000 metric tons of plastic from vehicles at the end of their lives are burned or sent to landfill in Europe. But this has to change, fast.
Under the EU’s proposed revision of its End-of-Life Vehicles Regulation (EU ELV), new vehicles will have to contain at least 15% recycled plastic within six years, rising to 25% within a decade, and at least a fifth of that material must have come from vehicles that have been scrapped.
With around 10.8 million new passenger cars registered in the EU in 2025 (20% of which are not made in Europe) and ​200–240 kg of plastic per vehicle, the 15% recycled content target implies the production of roughly 350,000 tons of recycled plastic annually.
At the moment, no more than 2.5% of plastic from end-of-life vehicles finds its way into new cars, so there is ‌a big gap.
A new initiative to tackle this shortfall has emerged – not from carmakers but from a group of chemicals companies.
The Global Impact Coalition (GIC), a platform focused on cutting carbon and introducing circularity into the chemicals sector, created a pilot project to show how a combination of mechanical and chemical recycling of plastic could help the automotive industry meet its targets.
The project involved eight companies from the chemicals and waste industries and saw 100 end-of-life vehicles put through a process of dismantling, shredding and sorting to see if plastic components could be recovered from old cars and turned into material that is good enough to be used again.
No single company in the automotive recycling chain has both the incentive ​and the capability to build this system unilaterally, so the entire value chain – from chemicals producers to carmakers to dismantlers and waste processors – needs to come together.
“The raw materials exist but the system to convert them into automotive-grade feedstock doesn’t,” says Charlie Tan, CEO of the ​GIC. “There is a gap between regulatory ambition and how prepared the current system is to meet those goals.”
The pilot proved that while it is technically feasible to recover and recycle plastics, there is still a long way ⁠to go on costs before a viable business case can be made. Nonetheless, says Tan, “the conversation is shifting from ‘can recycling automotive plastic work technologically’ to ‘can we build an economically viable supply chain and what would everyone’s role be?’”.
Although the pilot project was led by the chemicals sector, it is carmakers that ​sit at the heart of circularity. “What makes the automotive sector unique is that it has one of the biggest volume feedstocks that can be collected for chemical recycling,” says Ana Sofia Almagro, global projects lead at the GIC.
For plastics producers to scale up chemical recycling, they need long-term demand signals as well as ​a source of reliable, high-quality feedstock. Because of their need to use plastic recovered from old cars in new vehicles as a result of the new rules, automotive original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) provide both. “There is an unusually close link between the supply of recycled plastic and the demand from OEMs for recycled plastic,” says Almagro. “That could provide the demand signal that chemicals companies need to build facilities for more chemical recycling.”
The pilot project found that current sorting methods, and the make-up of many car parts, mean that the quality of recovered materials falls short of the requirements of today’s models. But with carmakers as both supplier and customer they can act to change that, says Dr Dirk Voeste, ​chief sustainability officer at Volkswagen.
“We’re looking at being more circular by design, and what that means. How do we design the car of the future not just to reduce the amount of polymers that we use, but also to make it easier to disassemble? If we design a part differently, we ​can save so much time at disassembly,” says Voeste.
Volkswagen is also working with the German government’s Open Hybrid Lab-Factory (OHLF), which is based in Wolfsburg, the company’s headquarters. OHLF’s research campus focuses on how to develop and produce materials that are resource-efficient, lightweight and circular.
VW brand Audi, through its Material Loop project, is looking at ways ‌to recycle not just ⁠plastics but also steel, aluminium and glass. There are well-established and successful recycling systems in place for these materials, but plastics are much harder to deal with.
Plastics recycled mechanically are weaker than virgin plastic and can only be recycled a few times. There are also problems mixing different plastics, which melt at different temperatures, with contamination and the growing amount of packaging that uses composite or multi-layer materials, which are difficult to separate.
“A key challenge for products that contain plastic is that they are very mixed together, and they have been bolted, welded or glued,” says Michael Puffer, head of alternative and new materials sourcing at chemicals producer Covestro. “It’s difficult to get material of a purity that it can be used as a feedstock for new products.”
Recycling plastic chemically offers more flexibility because it reduces plastic waste to chemical building blocks, which can be used to create virgin plastic. But currently there is just 0.29 million tons ​of chemical recycling capacity operational in Europe, Almagro says, with a pipeline ​of planned projects with a capacity of 2.8 million tons. This ⁠compares to the 53 million tons of plastic waste produced in the EU in 2019, which is forecast to double by 2060, surpassing 100 million tons a year. “What is stopping more capacity being built is a lack of credible demand signals, which is almost as important as the price of the feedstock,” says Puffer.
Chemicals companies are keen to build more chemical recycling capacity because they are under pressure to cut their own emissions. Covestro, for example, is ​committed to becoming fully circular, and “climate neutral” by 2050. But collaboration and partnerships will be key to accelerating progress, Puffer says.
“Circularity is a new business model,” says Voeste. “In the old days, we would design and produce ​a vehicle and then never see it again. ⁠Now, we want it back. We want spare parts, materials.
It’s a completely different way of thinking than the old linear model. There are untapped revenue pools that we have not seen before.” These range from remanufactured parts to reduced raw material, resource and energy use. Other potential revenue streams include second-life batteries and as-a-service and subscription models.
But carmakers are facing growing competition for low-carbon molecules, in particular from the shipping and aviation sectors. And the demand signals are not yet clear enough to scale up production, the goal of the next phase of GIC’s project.
A whole new digital infrastructure will also be needed to allow all parts of the value ⁠chain to trace used ​plastic on its journey to becoming new products, and to allow carmakers to show they are complying with the regulations. “We need some kind of digital passport for cars,” says Voeste. “If ​you know everything about a car, it will be much cheaper and easier to disassemble.” The new ELV regulation introduces, among other things, a Circularity Vehicle Passport – a digital record of a vehicle’s materials, components and circularity data.
Tan expects that there will be lessons for other sectors, ranging from shipping to fast-moving consumer goods and fashion. One area that Covestro has identified as ​very promising is mattresses. Some 44 million mattresses are disposed of every year in Europe, says Puffer, and they are full of polyurethane foam that can be repurposed.
But when it comes to scaling up plastic recycling and making its production more circular, the automative sector is expected to be the driving force.
